name: Cardiac output
seoDesc: Cardiac output: work out cardiac index from your height and your weight. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Cardiac output calculator turns your height, your weight and more into cardiac index. It suits an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Cardiac output calculator work?
sections.html:
The Cardiac output calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports cardiac index in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in your height, your weight, the hemoglobin and the oxygen tension (Arterial blood).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Cardiac output calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Cardiac index=((625 ÷ 449) × (10 ^ 11 ÷ 20) × (8980 × (10 ^ 9 ÷ 20) × (your height ^ 29 ÷ 40) × (your weight ^ 17 ÷ 40) ÷ (oxygen concentration − oxygen concentration)) ÷ ((your height ^ 29 ÷ 40) × (your weight ^ 17 ÷ 40)))
Body surface area=(449 ÷ 6250) × (10 ^ 9 ÷ 20) × (your height ^ 29 ÷ 40) × (your weight ^ 17 ÷ 40)
Oxygen saturation=(1 ÷ 13400) × (10 × oxygen concentration − 31 × oxygen tension) ÷ hemoglobin
Oxygen tension=(10 ÷ 31) × oxygen concentration − 13400 ÷ 31 × hemoglobin × oxygen saturation
Cardiac output=(8980 × (10 ^ 9 ÷ 20) × (your height ^ 29 ÷ 40) × (your weight ^ 17 ÷ 40) ÷ (oxygen concentration − oxygen concentration))
O 2 consumption=((449 ÷ 50) × (10 ^ 9 ÷ 20) × (your height ^ 29 ÷ 40) × (your weight ^ 17 ÷ 40))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.
  • Shown in square meters, and convertible to any of the 24 units on that chip.
  • Shown in percent, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.
  • Shown in torr, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.
  • Shown in minutes, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.
  • Shown in minutes, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Area, opening in square meters
  • Time, opening in minutes
  • Density, opening in grams per deciliter
  • %, opening in percent
  • Pressure, opening in torr
  • Volume, opening in liters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Cardiac output calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — your height, your weight and the hemoglobin — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Cardiac output calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns cardiac index, derived from your height, your weight and the hemoglobin. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Cardiac output calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for your height, your weight, the hemoglobin and the oxygen tension, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter your height in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Your height opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Cardiac output calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
